c.tagline: The pilgrimage endpoint of the Camino de Santiago, crowned by a baroque cathedral holding the apostle's relics

taxi.fare: Metered, roughly €3.90 flag fall plus per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard and reliable

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number that connects to police, fire, and ambulance

hood_landmark.Zona Nova (New Town / Ensanche): Rúa do Franco's shopping and dining strip
hood_landmark.San Lázaro: The Palacio de Congresos and modern convention district
hood_landmark.Zona Universitaria: University of Santiago de Compostela's historic campus buildings
hood_landmark.Fontiñas: Fontiñas' modern residential blocks and local markets

avoid.reason: Minor pickpocketing around the cathedral and Praza do Obradoiro during peak pilgrim months.

hood_desc: The granite-paved medieval core around the cathedral, packed with pilgrim albergues, tapas bars, and souvenir shops; the natural base for nearly every visitor.
The 19th-century commercial expansion just beyond the old walls, with wider streets, department stores, and everyday local life.
A modern district anchored by the convention center, mainly of interest for business travelers rather than sightseers.
The historic university quarter with grand academic buildings and a young, lively student atmosphere.
A residential, largely local neighborhood with little tourist infrastructure, useful mainly for longer stays or budget apartments.
lodging: Parador de Santiago - Hostal Reis Católicos

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Galicia.

transit.pay: Cash or contactless card on board; rechargeable travel card available
transit.note: The old town is pedestrian-only, so buses mainly serve outlying neighborhoods and the airport

train: Renfe high-speed and regional trains connect to A Coruña, Vigo, and Madrid
bus: ALSA and Monbus coaches connect to Galician towns and the rest of Spain

airport.name: Santiago-Rosalía de Castro Airport
airport.note: ~11 km (20 min) from downtown. Airport bus (Line 6A) or taxi.

transit.m: Line 6A bus to the city centre and the train and bus stations

tip.s: Not obligatory; rounding up is appreciated for guides and tours
tip.r: 5-10% for good service, not expected at casual bars

food.name: Pulpo a feira
food.desc: Octopus boiled in copper, snipped onto a wooden plate and dressed with paprika, coarse salt and green olive oil.

places.name: El Meson do Pulpo
places.note: House speciality is octopus a feira; the fried mussels and cheese flan are equally praised.

places.name: Pulperia Os Concheiros
places.note: Rustic pulperia locally famous for its octopus, away from the tourist crush.

places.name: Los Sobrinos del Padre Benito
places.note: Long-standing old-town joint known among locals for consistently good pulpo.

food.name: Tarta de Santiago
food.desc: Dense almond cake dusted with icing sugar through a stencil of the Cross of Saint James - the pilgrim's dessert.

places.name: Pasteleria Mercedes Mora
places.note: Historic old-town pastry shop selling the certified almond tart whole or by the slice.

places.name: Mercado de Abastos
places.note: Stalls sell homemade tarts alongside the produce; good for taking one away.

places.name: O Curro da Parra
places.note: Modern Galician kitchen with a refined house version of the classic almond cake.

food.name: Empanada gallega
food.desc: Flat two-crust pie of thin bread dough filled with tuna and onion, cockles, or pork - sold by the wedge everywhere.

places.name: Mercado de Abastos
places.note: The market bakeries turn out the day's empanadas; buy a wedge and eat it standing.

places.name: O Gato Negro
places.note: Tiny, gloriously old-fashioned tavern pouring wine in ceramic bowls with simple plates.

places.name: Bierzo Enxebre
places.note: Warm stone-walled dining room doing honest Galician and Bierzo home cooking.

food.name: Percebes
food.desc: Goose barnacles prised off Atlantic rocks by hand, briefly boiled in seawater - the most expensive and most prized bite in Galicia.

places.name: Mercado de Abastos
places.note: Buy shellfish at a stall and have a market kitchen cook it for you on the spot.

places.name: Pazo de Altamira
places.note: Well-regarded seafood restaurant on the market's doorstep; reliable percebes in season.

places.name: Restaurante Don Quijote
places.note: Long-established Galician seafood house just outside the old town walls.

food.name: Vieiras a la gallega
food.desc: Scallops baked in their fan-shaped shells with onion, paprika and breadcrumbs - the emblem of the Camino on a plate.

places.name: A Noiesa Casa de Comidas
places.note: Family-run comedor where the owner greets you; strong on classic Galician shellfish.

places.name: O Curro da Parra
places.note: Contemporary small plates that treat Galician seafood with a lighter hand.

places.name: Restaurante Don Quijote
places.note: Traditional preparation of scallops and other Rias Baixas shellfish.

food.name: Lacon con grelos and caldo gallego
food.desc: Salt-cured pork shoulder with bitter turnip greens and potatoes, and the peasant broth of greens, beans and pork fat.

places.name: O Gato Negro
places.note: Old-school tavern cooking of the sort that has all but vanished elsewhere in the centre.

places.name: Bierzo Enxebre
places.note: Hearty inland Galician dishes done properly, popular with locals in winter.

places.name: A Noiesa Casa de Comidas
places.note: Home-style casa de comidas with daily traditional stews and broths.

food.name: Albarino and Ribeiro wine
food.desc: Crisp Atlantic whites - saline Albarino from the Rias Baixas and lighter Ribeiro, still poured from a jug in old taverns.

places.name: O Gato Negro
places.note: Ribeiro served in traditional white ceramic cuncas; the most atmospheric wine stop in town.

places.name: Abastos 2.0
places.note: Market-side bar matching daily market produce with a sharp Galician wine list.

places.name: A Tafona
places.note: Michelin-starred modern Galician kitchen with a thoughtful regional wine pairing.

food.name: Queimada
food.desc: Orujo spirit set alight with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel while an incantation is read - Galicia's theatrical nightcap.

places.name: Restaurante Don Quijote
places.note: Prepares the flaming punch tableside, spell included, for groups after dinner.

places.name: Pazo de Altamira
places.note: Traditional end-of-meal queimada in a stone dining room beside the market.

places.name: O Dezaseis
places.note: Rustic cellar restaurant on the pilgrims' approach road; a favourite for long group dinners.

landmarks: Catedral de Santiago de Compostela
The soaring Romanesque-Baroque cathedral over the apostle James's tomb is the emotional climax of the Camino and home of the swinging Botafumeiro.
Praza do Obradoiro
Pilgrims collapse in triumph on this majestic granite square, encircled by the cathedral, royal hospital, palace and university facades.
Hostal dos Reis Católicos
Built by Ferdinand and Isabella in 1499 as a pilgrims' hospital, now a Parador hotel ranked among the world's oldest continually operating inns.
Mosteiro de San Martiño Pinario
Spain's second-largest monastery rewards visitors with a staggering Baroque facade and gilded altarpieces rivalling the cathedral next door.
Mercado de Abastos
Galicia's gastronomic soul: a 1941 granite market where fishmongers sell octopus and scarlet prawns that nearby stalls will cook on the spot.
Parque da Alameda
The city's beloved promenade park, whose Paseo da Ferradura viewpoint frames the classic postcard of the cathedral's spires above old-town rooftops.
Praza da Quintana
An austerely beautiful split-level square behind the cathedral, where the Holy Door opens only in Jacobean jubilee years.
Museo do Pobo Galego
Inside the convent of San Domingos de Bonaval, a famous triple spiral staircase leads through exhibits of Galician folk life and traditions.
Cidade da Cultura de Galicia
Peter Eisenman's undulating hilltop complex of flowing stone and glass, a striking contemporary counterpoint to the medieval city below.
Rúa do Franco & the Old Town
The stone-arcaded streets of the UNESCO-listed centre funnel pilgrims past pulpo taverns, silversmiths and centuries-old university halls.

train.note: No international trains - the Vigo-Porto line requires a change at the border and no through service runs to Santiago. Avril high-speed trains reach Madrid in about 3 hours, and the Galician Eje Atlántico line runs frequently south to Pontevedra and Vigo and north to A Coruña. The station is a 20-minute walk south of the cathedral. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: The bus station is northeast of the centre. ALSA runs the Portuguese services and the domestic network to A Coruña, Lugo, Vigo and Madrid, plus the useful buses to Finisterre and Muxía for pilgrims continuing past Santiago. Carry your passport or EU ID for Portugal.

ferry.note: Santiago is about 30 km inland with no port, so there are no ferries. The nearest passenger sailings are the ría boats around Vigo and the Cíes Islands, roughly an hour and a half south.

half.name: Cabo Fisterra
half.blurb: A rocky Atlantic headland historically thought to be the end of the known world, with a lighthouse and coastal cliffs.

half.name: Muxía
half.blurb: A fishing village on the Costa da Morte with a coastal sanctuary church and wave-battered rocks said to have mystical origins.

half.name: A Coruña
half.blurb: A port city with the Tower of Hercules, a working Roman-era lighthouse, and a glassed-in seafront promenade lined with galleries.

half.name: Padrón
half.blurb: A riverside town famous for small green peppers served fried and salted, and legends tying it to the arrival of Saint James's remains.

full.name: Islas Cíes
full.blurb: An uninhabited archipelago off Vigo protected as a national park, with white-sand beaches reached only by a limited-capacity ferry.

notes.walk: The old town is compact, pedestrianized, and very walkable; the cathedral square is the natural center of any visit
notes.card: Widely accepted; cash useful for small pilgrim albergues and market stalls
notes.safety: Very safe city, popular with solo pilgrims and travelers of all ages. Petty theft near the cathedral and train station is the main concern.
notes.religion: Roman Catholic (majority, reinforced by the pilgrimage tradition); no religious affiliation (growing minority)
notes.net: Strong 4G/5G coverage citywide. Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes. ~€10-20 for a 10-20GB prepaid tourist SIM. Free wifi widely available. A Movistar, Vodafone, or Orange tourist SIM or eSIM.
notes.transit: Tranvías de Santiago urban bus network
notes.transport: Santiago-Rosalía de Castro Airport (SCQ), about 20 min from the city. Renfe high-speed and regional trains connect to A Coruña, Vigo, and Madrid. ALSA and Monbus coaches connect to Galician towns and the rest of Spain. Well connected via the AP-9 motorway; not needed for the old town itself.
